questions.q: List every supporting character or group the speaker encounters or observes in "Refugee Blues," in the order they appear.
questions.a: The consul (stanza 4), the committee (stanza 5), the speaker at the public meeting (stanza 6), Hitler (stanza 7), the poodle in a jacket and the cat let in (stanza 8), the fish swimming in the harbour (stanza 9), the birds in the trees (stanza 9), and the ten thousand soldiers on the plain (stanza 11). A wrong answer that lists only the consul and Hitler reveals the student misses the poem's cumulative architecture—each encounter adds a distinct layer of exclusion (bureaucratic, procedural, rhetorical, ideological, domestic, natural, military). Missing the animals shows the student hasn't grasped Auden's central ironic strategy: non-humans possess the belonging denied to humans.

questions.q: Why does Auden include animals—the poodle, cat, fish, and birds—as "characters" in a poem about human refugees? What work do they do that human supporting characters cannot?
questions.a: The animals function as ironic foils who possess, by nature, the three things the refugees are systematically denied: shelter (poodle's jacket, cat's open door), freedom of movement (fish swimming "as if they were free"), and political innocence (birds with "no politicians"). They are not "characters" with agency but silent witnesses whose very existence condemns the human world. A wrong answer treating them as decorative imagery ("Auden likes nature") misses the structural role: each animal encounter tightens the circle of exclusion—first domestic comfort, then natural liberty, then the very category of "the human race" is shown to be a privilege, not a birthright.

questions.q: In stanza 6, the public meeting speaker says: "If we let them in, they will steal our daily bread." Identify the rhetorical strategy this character employs, and explain how the poem frames him as a type rather than an individual.
questions.a: The speaker employs scapegoating rhetoric—the zero-sum fallacy that refugee survival threatens citizen survival. He is framed as a type through: (1) no name or description, only "the speaker"; (2) the collective "we/our" claiming to voice the majority; (3) the dehumanizing "them" that mirrors the consul's "you." His function is to legitimize prejudice as democratic common sense. A wrong answer analyzing his "motives" or "personality" misses the allegorical mode—he is the embodied argument of xenophobia, not a person with psychology.

questions.q: Compare the consul (stanza 4) and the committee (stanza 5) as representatives of state power. How do their different modes—active hostility versus polite procedural delay—work together to trap the refugee?
questions.a: The consul exercises sovereign violence through language: "banged the table" performs authority; "officially dead" enacts civil death—the refugee exists biologically but not legally. The committee exercises bureaucratic violence through time: "politely" and "chair" simulate due process; "return next year" suspends the refugee in a present with no future. Together they form a pincer: the consul denies status, the committee denies process. The refugee cannot live (no papers) and cannot wait (no time). A wrong answer seeing them as "different personalities" misses their structural complicity—they are two faces of the same machine.

questions.q: "Hitler appears in only one stanza (7), yet he is the poem's most consequential supporting character." Defend or challenge this claim using evidence from the poem's structure and imagery.
questions.a: Defend. Hitler's single appearance—"thunder rumbling in the sky... saying: 'they must die'"—reframes every prior encounter as his instrument. The thunder metaphor makes him elemental, inescapable, preceding the storm. "We were in his mind" reveals the terrifying intimacy of genocidal intent: the refugee is not incidental but targeted. The consul's table, the committee's chair, the politician's bread—all serve this mind. Poetic compression means presence ≠ frequency; Hitler is the absent center organizing the poem's periphery. A wrong answer counting lines misses how lyric poetry works: one image can carry the weight of a system.

questions.q: Write a four-line stanza in the poem's ballad meter (loose abcb, four beats/three beats) that introduces a new supporting character: a border guard who checks the refugees' papers. Include the refrain "my dear" and show how this character extends the poem's logic of exclusion.
questions.a: Example: "The border guard unrolled the scroll / And read our names with heavy sigh: / 'No country claims you, not a soul,' / My dear, no country claims us, I." A strong answer maintains the meter, uses the refrain naturally, gives the guard a characteristic action (reading a list), and extends the logic: the consul declared them dead, the committee delayed them, the guard confirms their statelessness. A poor answer ignores meter, treats the refrain as decoration, or makes the guard sympathetic—missing that every supporting character in this poem serves the exclusionary system.
